traps.desc: read across to the ice-cream column and reported its largest figure instead

problems.desc: Written diagnosis of the causal claim. Full credit for saying that Ola has found an association, not a cause: the two columns rise together, but nothing in the table shows that buying ice cream produces rescues, and a table of totals can never show that on its own. Accept any wording that separates a pattern from a cause; correcting the number alone earns no credit.

Written third factor. Full credit for naming a lurking variable that would push both columns up at once, most naturally hot weather or a hot summer: heat sends more people to buy ice cream and more people into the water, so both numbers rise without either causing the other. Accept town size or a busy tourist season as alternatives, provided the response explains how the factor affects BOTH columns.

traps.desc: divided by the whole sample of 200 instead of the 60 instrument players

problems.desc: Written diagnosis. Full credit for saying that Jack used the wrong denominator: the question is about instrument players only, so the 45 must be divided by the 60 players in that group rather than by all 200 students surveyed. Accept any wording that names the correct denominator; giving only the corrected percentage earns no credit.

problems.slot: the mean score of the many-books group

problems.desc: Written judgement of the headline. Full credit for saying the headline is not justified: the survey shows only that the two groups differ, which is an association, and nobody changed how many books any student owned, so no cause has been demonstrated. Accept any wording that rejects the causal wording and points at the observational nature of the survey.

problems.slot: the mean score of the few-books group

problems.desc: Written proposal for better evidence. Full credit for describing an experiment rather than a survey: take a group of similar students, randomly decide which of them receive extra books, keep everything else the same, and compare the two groups' later scores. A response that instead names a confounding factor, such as family income or reading habits at home, and explains that it would have to be controlled, also earns full credit. A response repeating that the survey is not enough, with no proposal, earns partial credit.

traps.desc: subtracted the numbers of firefighters instead of the damage figures

problems.desc: Written diagnosis. Full credit for saying Rita has the direction backwards, or for naming town size as the factor behind both: larger towns have more and bigger fires, which is why they employ more firefighters and why they suffer more damage. Sending more firefighters does not create damage. Accept either the reversed-direction argument or the town-size argument, as long as it explains the pattern.

problems.slot: the mean of the sleep-schedule group
the mean of the comparison group
the difference between the two means

problems.desc: Written judgement comparing the two studies. Full credit for choosing the first study and explaining why: students were assigned to the two groups at random, so the groups started out alike and the only planned difference was the sleep schedule, which lets the eight-mark gap be attributed to it. The second study only observed students who had already chosen the app, so keener students could account for both the app and the higher scores. Accept any wording that contrasts random assignment with self-selection.
